statement: Ford-Fulkerson on a network with integer capacities terminates after at most m augmenting-path iterations (m = number of edges), no matter which augmenting paths are chosen.
definitions: Ford-Fulkerson = the generic augmenting-path method: repeatedly pick ANY s-t path with positive residual capacity in the current residual network (including reverse arcs created by earlier augmentations) and augment by its bottleneck; one iteration = one augmentation. Capacities are positive integers; the claim quantifies over all valid choices of paths.
ground_truth_witness: The classic 4-node network: s->a and s->b with capacity 1000, a->t and b->t with capacity 1000, and the middle arc a->b with capacity 1 (m = 5 edges, max flow 2000). An adversary that always augments along s->a->b->t and then along s->b->a->t (the second uses the residual arc b->a created by the first) pushes exactly 1 unit per iteration and needs 2000 augmentations. Every chosen path is a genuine augmenting path in the current residual graph, so this is a legal Ford-Fulkerson execution: the number of iterations scales with the capacity value, not with m.
reference_authority: online-cited counterexample (MO/MSE/CS.SE/Wikipedia) with verify script, verified per partB_feasibility records

skeptic.objection: Precise and false. Simulated the alternating augmentations on the 5-arc network: 2000 iterations of one unit each, each along a valid residual path, versus m = 5. The refutation requires choosing a network and arguing (by induction on the residual graph) that the adversarial path remains augmenting - a standard but genuine argument. Roster flow items (cb-fc-*) concern uniqueness of cuts/flows, not iteration counts; no duplicate.
